What is Bulk Crap Uninstaller?
Bulk Crap Uninstaller is a free, open-source tool designed to thoroughly remove unwanted applications from your Windows machine. Unlike the standard Windows uninstaller, BCU goes deeper, identifying and removing leftover files, registry entries, and other remnants that can silently accumulate and slow down your system.
Key Benefits for Developers:
  Lean Development Environment: Keep your system resources free for your development tools and applications. 
  Improved Performance: Faster boot times, quicker application launches, and a more responsive overall system.
  Thorough Cleanup: Ensures that no junk is left behind, preventing potential conflicts or performance degradation.
  Ease of Use: A user-friendly interface makes it simple to select and uninstall multiple applications at once.
By integrating BCU into your system maintenance routine, you invest in the efficiency and longevity of your development setup. It's a small step that can yield significant improvements in your daily workflow.
Conclusion
For any developer or power user looking to maintain a clean and efficient Windows environment, Bulk Crap Uninstaller is a highly recommended tool. Its open-source nature and powerful features make it an invaluable asset for anyone serious about system optimization.

articles.author: Naomi Ansah
articles.description:
When people talk about hosting portfolios, the usual recommendation is static hosting using platforms like Amazon S3, Vercel, Netlify, or CloudFront. And honestly, that’s often the right architectural choice.
 Network tab, and submitted the contact form from the live portfolio itself.
Seeing consistent 200 OK responses from a cloud-hosted backend felt very different from testing locally and made the entire system feel real.
What I Learned
This project helped me understand how backend services actually run on cloud servers, why process managers like PM2 are essential, and how Nginx fits into real production deployments. It also clarified the difference between simply running code and operating a service that needs to stay online.
More importantly, it gave me confidence working with Linux, AWS EC2, Node.js backends, Nginx, and production-style workflows. It also reinforced why managed services exist and how much complexity they quietly remove.
And that was exactly the goal.
If you’re early in your cloud journey and curious about what happens under the hood, I highly recommend trying something similar.

articles.title: Going Beyond Static Hosting: Deploying a Node.js Contact Form API on AWS EC2
